messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nabil, a 38-year-old Middle Eastern hairdresser living alone, came to understand his life as having split into “before” and “after” the day his body first betrayed him. The frightening event had been a sudden, life-threatening illness that struck while he was still at work in the salon, standing behind a client with scissors in hand when his chest tightened, sweat broke out across his back, and the room seemed to tilt. He remembered the metallic smell that seemed to cling to the air, the panic of being rushed through medical assessments, and the humiliation of lying under bright lights while strangers examined him as if he were already half gone. Since then, certain things had become loaded with danger in a way he could not shake: waking from a nightmare with his heart hammering and no immediate sense of where he was; seeing photos connected to the illness or the hospital period; and any medical examination or procedure. Each of these moments hit him with a wave of fear and horror so sudden that he felt pulled back into the same helplessness, his whole body tensing as if it had been warned that danger was immediate.

The memories did not come to him like ordinary recollection. Sometimes it was a smell that arrived first — a sharp, clinical odor that belonged to the hospital and would fill his mind before he could name where he was. At other times, the event returned as pain in the same places his body had hurt during the illness, making him clutch at his chest or stomach as though the illness were returning in real time. There were also moments when no clear picture came at all, only the full emotional force of that period: terror, shame, and the sense of being trapped inside a body he could not control. Those surges of memory were enough to drive his threat system into overdrive. Once the feelings hit, he became more vigilant, scanning himself for signs that something was wrong, and the tension in his muscles never fully settled. He had come to believe that his body kept acting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and that frightened him almost as much as the illness itself. He wondered, with growing alarm, whether these reactions meant he was going crazy, and whether he could still trust his own body at all.

That belief changed the way he moved through ordinary life. After one nightmare left him gasping awake and shaky for the rest of the morning, he found himself dreading sleep, but it was the daytime reminders that were hardest to avoid. In the salon, a client once brought in a photograph from a family gathering that happened to include a hospital bracelet on someone’s wrist, and Nabil felt his stomach drop before he had even processed what he was seeing. The sight pulled up the remembered smell, the bodily pain, and the same raw fear all at once, and he excused himself to the back room, shaking and ashamed. He began turning away from photos on customers’ phones and making sure he never lingered over anything medical. Even routine physical exams became a source of mounting distress; a recent appointment, meant to be simple, left him so activated that he left convinced the exam itself had confirmed his vulnerability. The more he noticed his body reacting, the more certain he became that his body was the enemy, and that certainty fed the fear again. He would catch himself checking his pulse, bracing against another wave, and those sensations would in turn bring the illness back into his mind.

Over the months, the memory of the illness and the fear of its return began to chase each other. A smell, a photo, or a medical setting could summon the full force of the event; once the memories flared, they sharpened his sense of threat and made the next trigger feel even closer. Nabil’s work suffered in quiet but concrete ways. He kept his schedule lighter, avoided conversations about health, and hesitated when clients mentioned hospitals, family illnesses, or photos from the time he had been sick. He had once been known for being relaxed and chatty in the chair, but now he stayed on guard, monitoring his own body for the first sign of distress. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the cycle and afraid that one more strong reaction would prove he could no longer trust himself. He wanted to feel safe in his own body again, but what finally brought him to therapy was the fear that, without help, he would keep living as though the illness were still happening.
